summary:
SHMS-26 is a web-based health monitoring console for astronauts on missions where Earth is minutes away and crews must interpret their own data. It combines astronaut telemetry, personal baselines, mission context (phase, gravity, communication delay), operator-configured warning limits and a library of NASA HRP and CSA research. From these it produces an interactive display for six health domains, each with an evidence panel that shows why it was assigned.

It addresses the challenge by making monitoring explainable and safe. SHMS-26 never gives an overall health score or a diagnosis, and it never invents thresholds or baselines. Baselines need at least three valid readings, and simulated data is always labeled and kept apart from operator data. It supports live heart-rate streaming from Bluetooth wearables, a mission simulator with six profiles, radiation dosimetry (including a reference card for the CSA CANS neutron spectrometer), and a guided tour.

SHMS-26 — Synchronized Health Monitoring System

AI-Enhanced Astronaut Health Monitoring and Human Spaceflight Intelligence Platform

1. Project Overview

SHMS-26 (Synchronized Health Monitoring System) is an AI-enhanced astronaut health monitoring and spaceflight intelligence platform designed to address one of the most important challenges of human space exploration: understanding and protecting astronaut health during missions beyond Earth.

As humanity prepares for increasingly ambitious missions to the Moon, Mars and beyond, astronauts face complex physiological, psychological and environmental challenges. Microgravity, radiation exposure, isolation, altered sleep cycles and prolonged exposure to unfamiliar environments can significantly affect human health and performance.

SHMS-26 aims to bring together astronaut health monitoring, scientific research, mission context and intelligent data analysis within one integrated platform.

The system's central objective is to transform complex astronaut health information into organised, understandable and explainable insights that can support astronauts, researchers and mission operators.

2. What Does SHMS-26 Do and How Does It Work?

SHMS-26 organises astronaut health and performance information into six interconnected domains:

  1. Cardiovascular health.
  2. Respiratory health.
  3. Physical condition.
  4. Recovery and rest.
  5. Psychological wellbeing.
  6. Environmental health.

The platform is designed to collect and synchronise available observations from supported data sources, including manual measurements, imported datasets and compatible wearable devices.

At the centre of the platform is the Human Spaceflight Intelligence Engine (HSIE).

HSIE connects physiological observations with individual baselines, historical measurements, mission conditions and configurable warning thresholds.

Rather than treating measurements as isolated numbers, the engine evaluates available information within its relevant context. It identifies changes, highlights potential areas requiring attention and explains the factors contributing to its assessments.

The platform also incorporates research references from NASA's Human Research Program and Canadian Space Agency resources, allowing users to explore scientific evidence associated with human-spaceflight health risks.

Additional capabilities include:

  • Radiation monitoring.
  • Interactive mission simulations.
  • Exercise and countermeasure tracking.
  • Crew wellbeing and communication tools.
  • Scientific research exploration.
  • AI-assisted information analysis.
  • Historical health and performance comparisons.

3. Benefits and Intended Impact

SHMS-26 aims to improve how astronaut health information is collected, organised, interpreted and communicated.

Its intended benefits include:

Synchronized health monitoring: Bringing relevant physiological observations and mission information together within a unified monitoring environment.

Improved situational awareness: Helping users understand changes in astronaut measurements in relation to personal baselines and mission conditions.

Identification of concerning changes: Highlighting deviations from established baselines and operator-configured thresholds for further review.

Research accessibility: Connecting health observations with relevant scientific investigations and NASA and CSA research resources.

Mission preparedness: Allowing users to explore different spaceflight environments, mission phases and potential challenges through interactive simulations.

Holistic astronaut wellbeing: Recognising that human health involves more than physical measurements by incorporating recovery, voluntary psychological self-reports and environmental conditions.

The broader ambition is to contribute towards more informed human-spaceflight operations and the development of intelligent monitoring systems for future lunar and interplanetary missions.

SHMS-26 is intended as a research and decision-support platform, not an autonomous medical diagnostic system.
